claims.text: An ultrathin, epitaxially aligned Nb interlayer at the W–Cu interface will increase the composite's thermal conductivity.
The Nb interlayer will preserve the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
The Nb interlayer will preserve the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
The baseline is a W–Cu composite with an unmodified W/Cu interface.
The intervention is deposition of a nanometric, epitaxially aligned Nb coating at the W–Cu interface.
Fusion-reactor service exposes relevant materials to high temperatures and strong irradiation.
The proposed W–Cu composite will be exposed to thermal cycling in the intended applications.
The ultrathin Nb layer will promote efficient electron coupling across the W–Cu interface.
The Nb layer will act as a diffusion barrier between W and Cu.
Improved electron transmission through the Nb interlayer will lower W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
Suppressing W–Cu interdiffusion will prevent degradation of mechanical properties.
Suppressing W–Cu interdiffusion will prevent degradation of irradiation resistance.
The Nb-coated composite will have higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The Nb-coated composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the uncoated baseline.
The Nb-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the uncoated baseline.
The predicted improvement will hold under fusion-reactor operating conditions.
Long-term stability and adhesion of the Nb interlayer are necessary for the proposed benefit.
The optimal Nb-layer thickness, uniformity, and long-term stability under irradiation and thermal cycling are not established.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires only a measurable thermal-conductivity increase, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to exceed an example threshold of 10% as falsifying. A statistically significant increase below 10% could therefore satisfy the prediction while also meeting the stated falsification condition.
